analysis.one_liner: Requires federal agencies to reduce pollution burdens on communities of color and low-income communities.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it was introduced with 13 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents, and died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Environmental Justice Act of 2019 would make it a legal duty of every federal agency to find and fix pollution and health hazards that fall disproportionately on communities of color, indigenous communities, and low-income communities. It would require regulators to weigh the combined pollution already affecting a neighborhood before issuing air or water permits, deny or tighten permits for repeat violators, publish demographic and health data for communities near pollution sources, and create new ways for residents to sue over discriminatory environmental practices.
analysis.who_benefits: People living in or near polluted areas — fenceline communities next to factories, refineries, highways, and waste sites, which are disproportionately communities of color and low-income communities. The bill gives them enforceable rights to information, public participation, and legal action, and requires regulators to account for the total pollution a neighborhood already carries before adding more.

how_it_helps.text: Requires each federal agency to make environmental justice part of its mission and to update an annual strategy identifying and mitigating disproportionately high health and environmental effects on populations of color, indigenous communities, and low-income communities [S3].

Amends the Clean Water Act and Clean Air Act so that permits for discharges and major air sources must account for cumulative impacts — the combined past, present, and foreseeable pollution in a geographic area — and permits cannot be issued or renewed without a reasonable certainty of no harm to general and sensitive populations [S3].

Requires permitting authorities to identify persistent violators of the Clean Air Act, and to deny permits to applicants whose plans to come back into compliance are inadequate or who keep violating after a prior redemption plan [S3].

Creates a private right of action under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act so individuals can sue to challenge discriminatory practices by federally funded programs, and preserves implied rights of action and common law claims under the major environmental statutes [S3].

Directs agencies to collect and publish health and demographic data on fenceline communities, translate public notices for limited-English populations, continue EPA environmental justice mapping and grant programs, and support community-based science [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Industrial facilities that emit into air and water — chemical plants, refineries, manufacturers, mines, and other permitted major sources — would face harder-to-get and harder-to-renew permits, cumulative impact analyses, and permit denials for repeat violations. Federal agencies would bear new reporting, data, and mitigation duties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Facilities holding air and water permits

drawbacks.text: The cumulative-impacts standard — 'a reasonable certainty of no harm' — is strict and difficult to prove, and it applies to permits the agency already grants. Manufacturers and utilities warned measures like this could slow or block projects for expansion and infrastructure in already-industrialized areas [S3].

The bill directs every federal agency to produce annual environmental justice strategies, progress reports, and translated public materials, a substantial administrative workload with $10 million a year authorized for community grant programs but no dedicated funding stream for agencies' own compliance costs [S3].

Expanded private rights of action would let individuals sue agencies and covered entities over environmental justice failures, which critics of such provisions say invites litigation and delays agency decisions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health benefits are real and concentrated on the people who currently carry the most pollution — the bill is aimed at communities where asthma, contaminated water, and toxic exposure stack up. The costs fall on permitted facilities and federal agencies, in slower or denied permits and heavier reporting. The main design risk is that the 'reasonable certainty of no harm' standard may be hard to apply consistently, which could make permitting unpredictable even for projects with modest impacts.

outcome.mechanism: Booker introduced the bill in July 2019 with 13 cosponsors, but the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee never took it up, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the Environmental Justice Act of 2019 in the Senate on July 23, 2019, joined by 13 cosponsors — 12 Democrats and 1 independent [S1][S4].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works; no further action appears in the record [S5].
The bill received no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Facilities that hold or seek air and water permits — chemical plants, refineries, and other major emitters — are better off, because the stricter cumulative-impact permit standards, persistent-violator rules, and new citizen suits were never enacted. Residents of heavily polluted communities gained nothing from the bill's failure.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 23, 2019 and held no hearing, markup, or vote on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Did not bring the bill to the Senate floor or negotiate its inclusion in any package; with no committee action, it never reached a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 Senate supporters were Democrats or the independent Bernie Sanders; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill was never taken up by the Republican-run committee or floor.

industries.industry: Major air emitters (refineries, chemical plants, power plants)
industries.note: The bill would require cumulative-impact analyses before issuing or renewing their permits, could force added controls or deny permits outright, and would deny permits to persistent violators. Their operating costs and expansion options rise; nearby residents breathe less pollution.

Clean Water Act permit conditions would tighten to require a reasonable certainty of no harm considering the water body's existing pollution load. Facilities in already-burdened watersheds would face new conditions or denials.

These industries operate under several of the 'covered Acts' (Surface Mining Control Act, Solid Waste Disposal Act) whose citizens suits and common law claims the bill would preserve, opening them to more litigation from affected residents.

Not an industry, but a concentrated interest: the bill's data collection, mapping, permit standards, and new rights of action all run in the direction of these residents' health and participation. The bill died, so they gained nothing.
